questions.question: Five friends A, B, C, D and E sit in a row facing north. Who sits in the middle? I. A is at the extreme left and E is at the extreme right. II. B is immediately to the left of E, and C sits between A and B.
options: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not
Either statement alone is sufficient
Neither statement is sufficient even together
questions.rationale: Even merged, C between A (seat 1) and B (seat 4) can sit at seat 2 or seat 3, giving both A-C-D-B-E (middle D) and A-D-C-B-E (middle C). Two arrangements survive, so the answer is not unique.

questions.question: Six persons A to F sit around a circular table facing the centre. Who sits opposite C? I. A sits opposite D, and B sits opposite E. II. E sits third to the right of C.
options: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not
Either statement alone is sufficient
Both statements together are needed, but neither alone
questions.rationale: Statement I fixes two opposite pairs, so the leftover pair must be C and F. Statement II works because third to the right in a six-seat circle is directly opposite, making E the answer. Each alone pins the asked seat.

questions.question: How is M related to K? I. K is the sister of L, and M is the mother of L. II. M has exactly two children, K and L.
options: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not
Either statement alone is sufficient
Both statements together are needed, but neither alone
questions.rationale: Statement I pins both link and gender: M is L's mother and K is L's sister, so M is K's mother. Statement II leaves M's gender unstated, so M could be K's mother or father.

questions.question: How is A related to B? I. B is the son of C, and C is the sister of A. II. A is the brother of C, and B is the son of C.
options: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not
Either statement alone is sufficient
Both statements together are needed, but neither alone
questions.rationale: Statement I leaves A's gender unknown, so A could be B's uncle or aunt. Statement II marks A male ('brother') and B as C's son, so A is definitely B's uncle.

questions.question: In a certain code language, what is the code for 'blue'? I. 'sky is blue' is written as 'pa qe ri'. II. 'blue ink dries' is written as 'ri ta ve'.
options: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not
Either statement alone is sufficient
Both statements together are needed, but neither alone
questions.rationale: Each sentence alone leaves 'blue' one of three unmatched codes. Merged, 'blue' is the only word common to both sentences and 'ri' is the only code common to both, so blue = ri.

questions.question: In a certain code language, what is the code for 'rain'? I. 'rain falls here' is written as 'do re me', and 'snow falls here' is written as 'do re fa'. II. 'heavy rain came' is written as 'me so la'.
options: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not
Either statement alone is sufficient
Both statements together are needed, but neither alone
questions.rationale: Statement I carries its own anchor: 'falls here' is shared with codes 'do re', leaving 'me' unmatched for 'rain'. Statement II has three words against three codes and no anchor, so it cannot name a code.

questions.question: What is Ravi's rank from the top in a class of 40? I. Ravi is 23rd from the bottom. II. Ravi is 8 ranks below Sunil, and Sunil is 10th from the top.
options: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not
Either statement alone is sufficient
Both statements together are needed, but neither alone
questions.rationale: Statement I: 40 - 23 + 1 = 18th. Statement II: 10 + 8 = 18th. Each gives a complete route to the same rank, so either alone suffices.

questions.question: How many students are there in the row? I. A is 15th from the left end. II. B is 20th from the right end, lies to the right of A, with exactly 6 students between them.
options: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not
Either statement alone is sufficient
Both statements together are needed, but neither alone
questions.rationale: Neither statement fixes both ends alone. Merged: A at 15, six students after, so B at 22 from the left; B is 20th from the right, giving total = 22 + 20 - 1 = 41.

questions.question: In which direction is point B with respect to point A? I. B is north of C, and C is east of A. II. B is 4 km north of D, and D is 3 km north of A.
options: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not
Either statement alone is sufficient
Both statements together are needed, but neither alone
questions.rationale: Statement I: east then north puts B strictly north-east of A regardless of distances. Statement II: a chain of two northward steps puts B directly north of A. Each fixes the asked bearing.

questions.question: How is F related to E? I. 'E @ F' holds, and '@' means 'is the mother of'. II. 'F # E' holds, and '#' means 'is the son of'.
options: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not
Either statement alone is sufficient
Both statements together are needed, but neither alone
questions.rationale: Statement I makes F a child of E but leaves F's gender open, so son or daughter both survive. Statement II states F is a male child of E, so F is E's son.
